newsitem.title: ROMANIA: FOCUS-IMF optimistic on Romania economy, loans.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-IMF optimistic on Romania economy, loans.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund's (IMF) chief negotiator for Romania said on Friday he was optimistic that the Balkan country's reform programme was on target to win fresh Fund credits later this month.

Poul Thomsen said the new centrist government's decision to stick to a 1997 inflation target of 90 percent in this week's budget was ambitious after a 30.7 percent leap in prices last month. Inflation last year reached 56.9 percent.

But he said ministers had shown their commitment to making up for delays in reforms under their leftist predecessors who were voted out of office last November. Price liberalisation, a realistic exchange rate and pledges to shut down inefficient industry showed the government meant business.
"The structural reforms in the government programme are comprehensive and bold. There is no doubt about that," Thomsen told Reuters at the end of a week-long monitoring mission.
He said last month's steep price rise was "considerably above what we expected. This is nothing that gives rise to alarm.

"As the price increases are a once and for all matter, We don't really know what underlying inflation is," he said. "Is 90 percent feasible? Yes, but it is an ambitious target now. We shall have to see as the programme develops."

Thomsen said Romania's chances of securing credits at the IMF's April 23 board meeting were "very good". He expected five quarterly tranches of about $80 million would be made available subject to two monitoring missions later in the year.
The IMF halted credits to Romania last year after complaining that the leftist government was hindering price liberalisation and restricting currency markets.
Thomsen said it was vital for parliament to proceed quickly with the budget, which also calls for the deficit to be reduced to 4.5 percent of gross domestic product from 5.8 percent.

He also praised plans to shut down 10 loss-making factories, including two large oil refineries, and 20 large poultry and pig farms. Subsidies to inefficient farms, he said, were "a major reason for failing to control inflation".
The centrist government embarked on talks with the IMF within weeks of its victory over ex-communists who had run Romania since the 1989 overthrow of dictator Nicolae Ceausescu.
The central bank also undertook almost immediately to free foreign exchange markets and tightened monetary policy to restore confidence in the falling leu currency.
President Emil Constantinescu has told Romanians they have no choice but to proceed with the same reforms that have entrenched market policies in Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.
He told state television on Thursday that Romania met the criteria for its longshot bid for early NATO membership, but its economy was too undeveloped for European Union membership.
"The economy is not functioning yet. But financial stability has been achieved which must now be supported by structural reforms."
Romania, he said, had emerged relatively unscathed from being a "testing ground" for east Europe's post-communist ills.

Despite 1990 ethnic conflicts, it had avoided a war like Bosnia, the failure in 1994 of pyramid investment schemes did not degenerate into Albania's social upheaval and a run this year on the leu currency produced no Bulgarian-style collapse.

Leftists now in opposition say the government is incapable of following through on promises to improve living standards, but have agreed not to block the budget. Trade unions have grumbled about austerity but protests have so far been limited.
Ministers were careful to juggle expenditure to increase funds for social security by 2.2 percent with the IMF's approval to cushion the effects on people buffeted by change.
